To burgle a place means to illegally enter a building — usually by breaking in — with the intention of committing a crime there, most commonly theft.

When someone burgles a house, an office, a shop, or any other building, three things are happening:

  1. They are entering without permission (often by breaking a lock, smashing a window, or sneaking through an unlocked entry).
  2. They are trespassing — they have no right to be there.
  3. They intend to commit a crime inside, almost always stealing something.

The person who does this is called a burglar. The crime itself is called burglary. The verb form — burgle — describes the action of committing this crime.

This is important: the object of burgle is always the place, never a person.

  • You burgle a house.
  • You burgle a museum.
  • You burgle an office.

You do not "burgle a person." If someone takes money directly from a person — by threatening them, for example — that is robbery, not burglary.

These three words confuse many learners, so understanding the difference is key.

  • Steal refers to the act of taking something that doesn't belong to you. The focus is on the item being taken. He stole a watch.
  • Rob means to take something from a person or place, often with force or threat. The focus is on the victim — whether a person or an institution. They robbed the bank. She was robbed at gunpoint.
  • Burgle means to break into a building to commit a crime. The focus is on illegally entering the building. Someone burgled our house while we were away.

All three can describe parts of the same event. A thief might burgle your house (break in), and in doing so steal your laptop (take it) — but unless they threatened you directly, they did not rob you.

One more useful distinction: burglary does not require anyone to be home. In fact, it commonly happens when no one is present. Robbery, on the other hand, typically involves a direct confrontation with a person.

Burgle is the standard form in British English.

In American English, people almost always say burglarize instead, which means exactly the same thing.

  • British: Our home was burgled.
  • American: Our home was burglarized.

Both are correct — they're just regional preferences. If you're writing for a global audience or are unsure, either works, but knowing both helps you understand either.

• Someone burgled the art gallery and took two paintings.
  • She returned from holiday to find that her apartment had been burgled.
  • Police believe the same group has been burgling homes in the area for months.
  • The store was burgled three times in one year.
  • He was convicted of burgling a series of offices downtown.

To burgle = to break into a building illegally, intending to commit a crime (usually theft).

The word focuses on the unlawful entry into a place, not on stealing from a person directly. The person who does it is a burglar; the crime is burglary. It is the standard British English term; Americans typically say burglarize.
